questions.q: Clustering is described as which type of learning method?
o: An unsupervised learning method, drawing references from input data without labeled responses
A semi-supervised method, using partly labelled data
A supervised learning method, using labelled training data
A reinforcement learning method, driven by rewards
questions.e: Clustering is basically a type of unsupervised learning method: an unsupervised learning method is one in which we draw references from datasets consisting of input data without labeled responses.

questions.q: Clustering is used as a process to find:
o: the optimal path through a search space
meaningful structure, explanatory underlying processes, generative features, and groupings inherent in a set of examples
the posterior probability of a hypothesis
the decision boundary between two labelled classes
questions.e: Clustering is used as a process to find meaningful structure, explanatory underlying processes, generative features, and groupings inherent in a set of examples.

questions.q: Clustering is formally defined as the task of dividing the population or data points into groups such that:
o: each group corresponds to one labelled class
each group has the same number of data points
data points in the same group are more similar to each other and dissimilar to data points in other groups
the groups overlap as little as possible in feature count
questions.e: Clustering is the task of dividing the population or data points into a number of groups such that data points in the same groups are more similar to other data points in the same group and dissimilar to the data points in other groups.

questions.q: Why is clustering described as very much important?
o: Because it removes noise from the dataset
Because it guarantees an optimal classification boundary
Because it determines the intrinsic grouping among the unlabelled data present
Because it reduces the dimensionality of the feature space
questions.e: Clustering is very much important as it determines the intrinsic grouping among the unlabelled data present.

questions.q: Which two clustering methods are introduced?
o: Hierarchical clustering and spectral clustering
K-means clustering and hierarchical clustering
K-means clustering and density-based clustering
Partitional clustering and fuzzy clustering
questions.e: The two clustering methods introduced are K-means clustering and hierarchical clustering; the detailed treatment covers K-means.

questions.q: In the K-means worked example, which distance measure is used to assign points to the closest centroid?
o: Hamming distance, since the features are binary
Manhattan distance, which is always the most appropriate
Cosine similarity, since the data is high-dimensional
Euclidean distance, though in other scenarios other parameters may be more appropriate
questions.e: Closest centroid is a relative term; Euclidean distance is used here, but in other scenarios some other parameters may be more appropriate.

questions.q: Geometrically, what do the points on the line midway between two centroids have in common?
o: They become the new centroids on the next iteration
They are equidistant from the two centroids, which makes clear which points belong to which cluster
They belong to neither cluster and are discarded
They are always assigned to the first cluster
questions.e: We know from geometry that the points on the dividing line are equidistant from the two centroids; this makes it clear which points will belong to cluster 1 and which to cluster 2.

questions.q: How are the new centroids computed in each K-means iteration?
o: By computing the average, or centre of gravity, of all the points in each cluster except the centroid itself
By averaging the old centroid with the cluster's furthest point
By selecting the data point furthest from the previous centroid
By selecting a new random point from the dataset
questions.e: The new centroids are computed for each cluster by computing the average or centre of gravity of all the points except the centroid itself in each cluster.

questions.q: After new centroids are assigned and some points turn out to be in the wrong cluster, what does the algorithm do?
o: It increases the number of clusters by one
It recolours those points to the correct cluster and goes back to the reassignment step
It stops, because the centroids have been computed
It discards the misplaced points from the dataset
questions.e: The misplaced points are recoloured to assign them to the correct cluster; since reassignment has taken place, the algorithm goes back to step 4 and recomputes the centre of gravity for the new clusters.

questions.q: When has the K-means algorithm converged?
o: When all centroids coincide
When each cluster contains exactly one point
When the number of iterations reaches ten
When no data points need to be reassigned
questions.e: When no data points need to be reassigned, the algorithm has converged.

questions.q: What is the principal drawback of the standard K-means algorithm?
o: It requires labelled training data
It cannot handle more than two clusters
It is sensitive to the initialization of the centroids or mean points
It always converges to the global optimum
questions.e: One disadvantage of the K-means algorithm is that it is sensitive to the initialization of the centroids or the mean points.

questions.q: What can go wrong if a centroid is initialized to a far-off point?
o: It immediately becomes the global optimum
All points will be assigned to that centroid
The algorithm will refuse to run
It might end up with no points associated with it, while more than one cluster ends up linked with a single centroid
questions.e: If a centroid is initialized to be a far-off point, it might just end up with no points associated with it, and at the same time more than one cluster might end up linked with a single centroid. Similarly, more than one centroid might be initialized into the same cluster, resulting in poor clustering.

questions.q: What happens if more than one centroid is initialized into the same cluster?
o: The algorithm detects and corrects it
The number of clusters is reduced by one
Poor clustering results
The clusters merge automatically
questions.e: More than one centroid might be initialized into the same cluster, resulting in poor clustering; a poor initialization of centroids resulted in poor clustering in the illustrated example.

questions.q: When two different runs of K-means begin from different initial centroids, what is observed?
o: The number of clusters changes between runs
The clusters formed are always identical
The clusters formed are different based on the different initial centroids
The algorithm fails to converge in one of the runs
questions.e: Comparing two K-means solutions, the clusters formed are different based on different initial centroids, which is the random initialization problem.

questions.q: Which algorithm is the solution to the random initialization problem in K-means?
o: DBSCAN
K-means++
Hierarchical clustering
K-medoids
questions.e: The solution to the random initialization problem is the k-means++ algorithm; Python takes care of this and implements the k-means++ algorithm.

questions.q: In K-means++, how is the first centroid chosen?
o: As the mean of all data points
As the point furthest from the dataset's centre
As the first row of the dataset
Randomly, from the data points
questions.e: In K-means++ the first centroid is selected randomly from the data points; then for each data point its distance from the nearest previously chosen centroid is computed, and the next centroid is selected such that the probability of choosing a point is directly proportional to that distance.

questions.q: In K-means++, how is each subsequent centroid chosen?
o: With probability inversely proportional to the point's distance from the nearest centroid
Uniformly at random from the remaining points
As the point closest to the previously chosen centroid
With probability directly proportional to the point's distance from the nearest previously chosen centroid
questions.e: The next centroid is selected from the data points such that the probability of choosing a point as centroid is directly proportional to its distance from the nearest previously chosen centroid - so the point having maximum distance from the nearest centroid is most likely to be selected next.

questions.q: In K-means++, which point is most likely to be selected as the next centroid?
o: The point nearest the overall data mean
The point having the minimum distance from the nearest centroid
The point having the maximum distance from the nearest previously chosen centroid
A point chosen with equal probability to all others
questions.e: Because the probability is directly proportional to the distance from the nearest previously chosen centroid, the point having maximum distance from the nearest centroid is most likely to be selected next as a centroid.

questions.q: In K-means++, how many centroids are sampled before the procedure stops?
o: Two centroids
One centroid per data point
As many as the number of features
k centroids
questions.e: Steps 2 and 3 - computing distances and selecting the next centroid with probability proportional to distance - are repeated until k centroids have been sampled.

questions.q: Apart from the initialization, how does K-means++ differ from standard K-means?
o: It uses a different distance measure throughout
It never reassigns points once they are placed
It recomputes the number of clusters at each iteration
It does not differ: the rest of the algorithm is the same as standard K-means
questions.e: Apart from initialization, the rest of the algorithm is the same as the standard K-means algorithm: K-means++ is the standard K-means algorithm coupled with a smarter initialization of the centroids.

questions.q: What benefit does K-means++ provide?
o: It guarantees convergence in a single iteration
It removes the need to choose the number of clusters
It makes the algorithm supervised rather than unsupervised
It ensures a smarter initialization of the centroids and improves the quality of the clustering
questions.e: K-means++ ensures a smarter initialization of the centroids and improves the quality of the clustering.

questions.q: In the mall customer dataset used for the Python implementation, which fields are available?

Customer ID, gender, age and purchase decision
Outlook, temperature and play
questions.e: The mall dataset contains customer ID, gender, age, annual income and spending score from 1 to 100, where a lower score represents less spending and a higher score higher spending; the goal is to identify patterns within the customers.

questions.q: In the mall dataset, what does the spending score represent?
o: The number of purchases the customer has made
The customer's total annual spending in currency units
A value from 1 to 100 where a lower score means less spending and a higher score means higher spending
The probability that the customer will buy again

questions.q: Why is a dependent variable created for the mall clustering problem?
o: Because the spending score must be converted to a class
Because the dataset already contains a label that must be renamed
Because this is unsupervised learning with nothing known to predict, so a cluster number is created to represent the class based on the independent variables
Because the clustering algorithm requires labelled training data

questions.q: Why are only two independent variables selected for the mall clustering example?
o: Because the results need to be visualized, which can only happen for a dataset with two independent variables
Because K-means cannot handle more than two dimensions
Because the other variables contain missing values
Because the other variables are categorical

questions.q: Why is the customer ID discarded in the mall clustering example?
o: Because it is of no importance to the clustering task
Because it is a continuous variable
Because it duplicates the spending score
Because it contains missing values

questions.q: What metric is introduced to judge whether a certain number of clusters provides an optimum solution?
o: The within cluster sum of squares
The Davies Bouldin index
The silhouette coefficient
The Calinski Harabaz index
questions.e: A metric is needed to identify that a certain number of clusters in a dataset provides an optimum solution, and preferably it should be quantifiable; that metric is the within cluster sum of squares. Note that it is written both WCSS and, on one slide, WCCS.

questions.q: In the within cluster sum of squares formula, what do C1, C2 and C3 and Pi denote?
o: C1, C2 and C3 are the cluster labels, and Pi is the purity of cluster i
C1, C2 and C3 are the cluster sizes, and Pi is the probability of cluster i
C1, C2 and C3 are the centroids of clusters 1, 2 and 3, and Pi is the ith data point in the respective cluster
C1, C2 and C3 are the data points, and Pi is the centroid of cluster i
questions.e: C1, C2 and C3 are the centroids of cluster 1, cluster 2 and cluster 3 respectively, and Pi is the ith data point in the respective cluster.

questions.q: Why is the within cluster sum of squares very large when k = 1?
o: Because the centroid coincides with every data point
Because the metric is undefined for a single cluster
Because the single centroid is far away from the data points, so the distances are large
Because there are no distances to compute with one cluster
questions.e: With the solution for k = 1, computing WCSS gives quite a large value since the centroid is away from the data points Pi, so the distance between the centroid and the data points is large.

questions.q: What happens to the within cluster sum of squares as the number of clusters increases from 1 to 2?
o: It decreases, because the distance is computed within each cluster and need not reach the middle of the whole dataset
It stays the same, because the data has not changed
It becomes undefined until k reaches 3
It increases, because there are more centroids to account for
questions.e: With two centroids, the distance is computed within each cluster and does not need to reach all the way to the middle of the whole dataset, so the value of WCSS decreases compared with having only one cluster.

questions.q: What is the maximum possible number of clusters in K-means, and what is the WCSS at that limit?
o: Ten, at which the WCSS reaches its minimum
The number of data points, at which the WCSS reaches zero
The number of features, at which the WCSS reaches one
Unbounded, so the WCSS never reaches zero
questions.e: The maximum number of clusters can be equal to the number of data points; if we reach that maximum limit, the WCSS will reach a value of zero.

questions.q: In the illustrated WCSS chart, what is the drop in WCSS as k increases from 1 to 2?
o: About 8000 units, from 8000 to 0
About 2000 units, from 3000 to 1000
About 300 units, from 1000 to 700
About 5000 units, from 8000 to 3000
questions.e: The chart shows WCSS starting high and decreasing substantially: from k = 1 to 2 the decrease is 8000 - 3000 = 5000; from 2 to 3 it is 3000 - 1000 = 2000; and from 3 to 4 it is 1000 - 700 = 300.

questions.q: In the illustrated WCSS chart, what is the drop in WCSS as k increases from 2 to 3?
o: About 700 units, from 1000 to 300
About 300 units, from 1000 to 700
About 2000 units, from 3000 to 1000
About 5000 units, from 8000 to 3000
questions.e: From k = 2 to k = 3 the decrease in units on the y-axis is 3000 - 1000 = 2000.

questions.q: In the illustrated WCSS chart, what is the drop in WCSS as k increases from 3 to 4?
o: About 5000 units, from 8000 to 3000
About 300 units, from 1000 to 700
About 700 units, from 1000 to 300
About 2000 units, from 3000 to 1000
questions.e: From k = 3 to k = 4 the decrease in units on the y-axis is 1000 - 700 = 300, which is much smaller than the earlier drops.

questions.q: The elbow method determines the optimal number of clusters by looking for:
o: the point where the number of clusters equals the number of features
the point where the change in units goes from being substantial to not substantial
the point where the WCSS first becomes zero
the point where the WCSS is at its maximum
questions.e: Since the change in WCSS was large in the beginning and low at the end, we can use the elbow method to determine the optimal number of clusters: look for the point where the change in units goes from being substantial to not substantial.

questions.q: In the mall customer example, what value of k does the elbow method select?

questions.q: Which three evaluation metrics for clustering are identified?
o: WCSS, elbow point and inertia
Silhouette score, Calinski Harabaz index and Davies Bouldin index
Entropy, information gain and Gini index
Accuracy, precision and recall
questions.e: There are three commonly used evaluation metrics: the silhouette score, the Calinski Harabaz index and the Davies-Bouldin index.

questions.q: What does silhouette analysis study?
o: The number of iterations until convergence
The purity of each cluster relative to known labels
The variance within each feature
The separation distance between the clusters formed by the algorithm
questions.e: To study the separation distance between the clusters formed by the algorithm, silhouette analysis could be used.

questions.q: How is the silhouette coefficient calculated?
o: By summing the squared distances to each centroid
By counting the misclassified samples
By dividing the between-cluster variation by the within-cluster variation
By using the mean of the distance of the intra-cluster and nearest cluster for all the samples
questions.e: The silhouette coefficient is calculated by using the mean of the distance of the intra-cluster and nearest cluster for all the samples, as (nc - ic) divided by max(ic, nc), where ic is the mean intra-cluster distance and nc the mean nearest-cluster distance.

questions.q: In the silhouette formula (nc - ic) / max(ic, nc), what do ic and nc denote?
o: ic is the mean of the intra-cluster distance and nc the mean of the nearest-cluster distance
ic is the inner centroid and nc the nearest centroid
ic is the within-cluster variation and nc the between-cluster variation
ic is the number of clusters and nc the number of data points
questions.e: In the formula (nc - ic)/max(ic, nc), ic is the mean of the intra-cluster distance and nc is the mean of the nearest-cluster distance.

questions.q: What is the range of the silhouette coefficient?
o: From 0 to infinity
From minus 1 to plus 1
From minus infinity to plus infinity
From 0 to 1
questions.e: The silhouette coefficient ranges from -1 to 1; the closer to +1, the more separation between clusters.

questions.q: What does a silhouette coefficient close to plus 1 indicate?
o: That the sample lies on the decision boundary
That the clusters are perfectly overlapping
More separation between the clusters
That the sample may have been assigned to the wrong cluster
questions.e: The higher the silhouette coefficient - the closer to +1 - the more separation there is between clusters.

questions.q: What does a silhouette value of 0 indicate?
o: That the sample is on or very close to the decision boundary between two neighboring clusters
That the sample is at the centre of its cluster
That the sample was assigned to the wrong cluster
That the clustering is optimal
questions.e: A silhouette value of 0 indicates that the sample is on or very close to the decision boundary between two neighboring clusters.

questions.q: What does a negative silhouette value indicate?
o: That those samples might have been assigned to the wrong cluster
That the number of clusters is too small
That the clusters are maximally separated
That the sample lies exactly on a cluster boundary
questions.e: A negative silhouette value indicates that those samples might have been assigned to the wrong cluster.

questions.q: On what principle is the Calinski Harabaz index based?
o: The sum of squared distances to each centroid
The mean of intra-cluster and nearest-cluster distances
The principle of within-cluster and between-cluster distances
The principle of variance ratio, calculated between within-cluster diffusion and between-cluster dispersion
questions.e: The Calinski Harabaz index is based on the principle of variance ratio; this ratio is calculated between two parameters, within-cluster diffusion and between-cluster dispersion.

questions.q: For the Calinski Harabaz index, what indicates better clustering?
o: A lower index
An index equal to one
An index equal to zero
A higher index
questions.e: The higher the Calinski Harabaz index, the better the clustering.

questions.q: In the Calinski Harabaz formula, what do W(k) and B(k) denote?
o: W(k) is the within cluster variation and B(k) the between cluster variation
W(k) is the weight of cluster k and B(k) its bias
W(k) is the within-cluster distance and B(k) the nearest-cluster distance
W(k) is the number of clusters and B(k) the number of data points
questions.e: In the formula, n is the number of data points, k the number of clusters, W(k) the within cluster variation and B(k) the between cluster variation.

questions.q: On what principle is the Davies Bouldin index based?
o: The principle of within-cluster and between-cluster distances
The sum of squared errors from each centroid
The mean silhouette width across all samples
The principle of variance ratio
questions.e: The Davies Bouldin index is based on the principle of within-cluster and between-cluster distances; it is commonly used for deciding the number of clusters in which the data points should be labeled.

questions.q: How does the Davies Bouldin index differ from the other two metrics in interpretation?
o: Its value is not comparable across datasets
Its value should be small, so the main motive is to decrease it
Its value should be large, like the other two
Its value should be exactly one
questions.e: The Davies Bouldin index is different from the other two, as the value of this index should be small; so the main motive is to decrease the DB index.

questions.q: In the Davies Bouldin formula, what does Dij denote?
o: The distance between data points i and j
The within-to-between cluster distance ratio for the ith and jth clusters
The variance ratio between clusters i and j
The silhouette coefficient of sample i in cluster j
questions.e: Dij is the within-to-between cluster distance ratio for the ith and jth clusters; C is the number of clusters and i and j are numbers of clusters which come from the same partitioning.

questions.q: Why is the within cluster sum of squares described as a good metric for comparing K-means solutions?
o: Because it is quantifiable and can be compared across different values of k
